content: The analysis compared the diagnostic accuracy of Xpert Ultra and Xpert MTB/RIF for detecting pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) and rifampicin resistance. Nine studies involving 3,881 participants evaluated both tests for pulmonary TB detection, with Xpert Ultra also assessed using a composite reference standard that included clinical components defined by the primary study authors. For rifampicin resistance detection, eight studies with 1,039 participants evaluated Xpert Ultra. One study provided data for two cohorts, classified as separate studies (Mishra 2019a and Mishra 2019b). Most studies were judged to have high certainty of evidence. For detecting active TB in adults with pulmonary TB symptoms, systematic reviews assessed whether Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra should be used as initial diagnostic tests. Among children with pulmonary TB symptoms, studies evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of Xpert MTB/RIF compared to microbiological reference standards (MRS) and composite reference standards (CRS). The initial search identified 836 records, of which 707 were excluded. After full-text review, 50 studies were included in the meta-analysis, with 80% conducted in high TB burden countries and 20% in high TB/HIV burden countries. Forty-three studies evaluated Xpert MTB/RIF in children for pulmonary TB detection, and three studies assessed both Xpert Ultra and Xpert MTB/RIF. Most studies used culture as the reference standard, while one relied on smear microscopy. In terms of methodological quality, 83% of studies evaluating pulmonary TB had a low risk of bias in patient selection, and all studies had a low risk of bias in the index test domain. In the flow and timing domain, 88% of studies were judged to have a low risk of bias. However, 47% of studies had an unclear risk of bias in the reference standard domain due to reliance on a single culture to exclude TB. All studies using composite reference standards had unclear risk of bias due to imperfect accuracy and varying definitions of the composite standard. For applicability, 50% of studies had high or unclear risk of bias in patient selection because participants were exclusively inpatients at tertiary care centers or the clinical setting was unclear. Most studies (72%) had low concern regarding the applicability of the index tests due to standardized application. Eleven studies evaluating stool as a specimen for Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra had unclear risk of bias due to the absence of a standardized stool preparation protocol. The reference standard's applicability was considered low concern in 93% of studies. For rifampicin resistance detection, six studies (223 participants) evaluated Xpert MTB/RIF in high TB and multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) burden countries. Half of these studies had a low risk of bias in patient selection, and all had a low risk of bias in the reference standard domain. However, concerns about patient selection applicability arose due to exclusive enrollment from inpatient or tertiary care centers. The meta-analysis included 23 studies (6,612 participants) evaluating sputum specimens, 14 studies (3,468 participants) evaluating gastric specimens, four studies (1,125 participants) evaluating nasopharyngeal specimens, and 11 studies (1,592 participants) evaluating stool specimens. All these studies assessed Xpert MTB/RIF alone. Three studies (753 participants) evaluated both Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra on frozen sputum specimens, and one study (195 participants) evaluated both tests on nasopharyngeal specimens. No studies evaluated Xpert Ultra alone. For extrapulmonary TB detection, 65 studies were included, with 63 evaluating Xpert MTB/RIF and five assessing both Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra. These studies evaluated various specimens, including cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), lymph node aspirates, pleural fluid, urine, synovial fluid, peritoneal fluid, pericardial fluid, and blood. Sixty percent of studies were conducted in high TB burden countries, and 63% in high TB/HIV burden countries. Risk of bias was low in patient selection, index test, and flow/timing domains but high or unclear in the reference standard domain due to decontamination of sterile specimens before culture inoculation. For children with extrapulmonary TB, six studies (210 participants) evaluated Xpert MTB/RIF for lymph node TB diagnosis against MRS, and two studies (105 participants) used CRS. For TB meningitis, six studies (241 participants) evaluated Xpert MTB/RIF against culture on CSF, and two studies (155 participants) used CRS. The certainty of evidence was very low for sensitivity and low for specificity in detecting TB meningitis and lymph node TB. No studies evaluated Xpert Ultra for these conditions. For repeated Xpert Ultra tests in adults with pulmonary TB symptoms and an initial trace result, limited data prevented meta-analysis. Evidence was downgraded for inconsistency and imprecision, with very low certainty for sensitivity and specificity. For children, five studies (2,119 participants) evaluated multiple Xpert MTB/RIF tests compared to a single test. Concerns about indirectness arose due to enrollment from tertiary care settings, potentially including children with advanced disease. Certainty of evidence was very low for sensitivity and moderate for specificity. For adults with pulmonary TB symptoms or chest radiograph abnormalities, six surveys evaluated Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra against culture. Evidence was downgraded for indirectness and imprecision, with low certainty for sensitivity and moderate for specificity. For two Xpert Ultra tests versus one, three surveys (5,080 participants) showed very low certainty for sensitivity and moderate for specificity due to indirectness and imprecision. Overall, the studies highlight the diagnostic utility of Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra for TB and rifampicin resistance, with varying levels of evidence certainty depending on the population, specimen type, and test application.
